newsitem.title: USA: NYC asks Albany to approve new borrowing agency.
newsitem.headline: NYC asks Albany to approve new borrowing agency.

text.p: New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani on Tuesday urged state lawmakers to approve a new borrowing agency for the city as a way of circumventing a constitutional limit on how much debt it can issue.

"This will ensure that all of the additional capital dollars are made available to the Board (of Education) and that all of the city's vital capital needs are met. These issues cannot wait until the end of the session, but must be addressed as early as possible," Giuliani told the Joint Legislative Fiscal Committees, according to a draft text of his speech.
The mayor predicted that without the new Infrastructure Finance Authority, which would sell bonds to pay for schools and transportation, the city's capital program "will soon come to a halt."
The city is expected to hit its debt cap about a month before the end of its 1997 fiscal year on June 30.
City Council Speaker, Peter Vallone, a Democrat, also pressed the state legislature to swiftly approve the new agency, which Albany declined to do in a special session held in late December.
Vallone also asked the lawmakers to extend the city's personal income tax surchare, which Albany let expire at year-end.
The approximately $450 million in tax revenue raised by the surcharge mainly goes to help pay for the city's anti-crime program, called Safe Street/Safe City.

"Without it, the city will face enormous fiscal pressure to reduce police staffing and eliminate related programs in other agencies, thereby reversing the tremendous public safety gains we have achieved in recent years," Vallone said, in prepared comments.
The Republican mayor seemed willing to take at least some of the credit for two achievements that Gov George Pataki has viewed as some of his main accomplishments.

"Our local economic development efforts have helped create almost 110,000 private sector jobs and the welfare rolls have declined by more than 220,000 in the last 24 months," Giuliani said. Pataki, a Republican who has had a thorny relationship with the mayor, has said state-wide welfare rolls have fallen by over 250,00.
Giuliani urged the state legislature to modify the following aspects of the $66.1 billion state budget that Gov George Pataki has proposed.
--Proposed having the state fund and not cut reimbursement for special educational services in summer.

--Proposed having the city pay $10 million in administrative costs to collect income taxes in return for its accepting state reimbursement for the "actual costs" of housing state prionsers and providing associate degree programs at three colleges.
--Criticized cutting funds for probation by 13 percent, saying this eventually will cost the state more than it will save.

--Noted a plan to give school districts instead of counties the responsibility for a state-mandated program that educates three- to five-year old children with disabilities will mean lower reimbursement rates for busing these children, and clashes with Pataki's plan to cut property taxes.
